analysis.one_liner: Would end free hardrock mining on public lands by charging royalties and requiring cleanup plans.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 244-166 in November 2007, but the Senate committee never acted, and the bill died without a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Hardrock mining on federal land still operates under an 1872 law: companies claim gold, silver, copper, and other metals on public land, pay no royalty on what they take, and can buy the land outright. This bill would have charged an 8% royalty on new mining, required cleanup bonds and permits before digging, and steered the money toward cleaning up hundreds of thousands of abandoned mines that pollute western streams. The House passed it; the Senate never voted.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently get nothing when companies extract metals from public land and are often left holding cleanup bills for abandoned mines. Communities and tribes near mines would gain a fund for polluted water and public services, and everyone who uses public lands would gain from stricter permits and protected areas.

how_it_helps.text: The bill charges an 8% royalty of gross income on new hardrock production on federal land — the same general arrangement that has long applied to oil, gas, and coal — with a 4% rate for existing operations [S3, S4].

It requires mine operators to post financial assurance covering full reclamation, including the projected cost of water treatment after the mine closes, so taxpayers are not left with the bill [S3, S4].

It creates a Locatable Minerals Fund, fed by royalties and fees, with an account for cleaning up abandoned mines and another for community impact assistance to states, local governments, and Indian tribes [S3, S4].

It closes wilderness study areas, wild and scenic river areas, roadless areas, and other special places to new mining claims, and lets states, local governments, and tribes petition to withdraw land for drinking-water watersheds, wildlife habitat, or cultural values [S3, S4].

It requires federal permits before surface-disturbing mining, blocks permits that would cause 'undue degradation' or impair national parks and monuments, and denies permits to operators with a pattern of willful environmental violations [S3, S4].
It authorizes citizen suits to enforce the Act and lets states keep stricter rules of their own [S3, S4].

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies, which would pay royalties, claim-maintenance fees, permit costs, and cleanup bonds for the first time under the 1872 law. Consumers could see modestly higher prices for metals, and some mining in protected areas would never happen.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

drawbacks.text: An 8% royalty and full-cost cleanup bonds raise the cost of domestic mining, which can push some production to countries with weaker environmental rules and can raise input costs for U.S. manufacturing and for technologies that use mined metals [S3].

The permitting structure — exploration permits, operations permits, financial assurance, and monitoring — adds significant regulatory burden, and smaller claim holders would face compliance costs even though claim-maintenance fees are waived for those holding ten claims or fewer [S3].
Critics of pre-1994 patent claims would note that the bill still allows patents for applications filed on or before September 30, 1994, grandfathering some land disposal at 1872-era terms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is substantial: hardrock mining is the last major extractive use of federal land with no royalty, and abandoned mines impose real, ongoing cleanup and water-contamination costs on taxpayers and communities. The costs fall on the mining industry, with some risk of higher metals prices and some production shifting abroad. On balance the bill would have shifted a long-standing public subsidy and public liability back onto the industry that creates it.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 244-166 on November 1, 2007, but the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee never took it up, and the 110th Congress ended without a Senate vote.

narrative.text: Introduced in May 2007 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which held subcommittee hearings in July and October and marked the bill up on October 18 and 23 [S7].
The committee ordered the bill reported amended on a 23-15 vote, and it was reported and placed on the Union Calendar on October 29 [S7].

The House debated it under a rule on November 1, 2007; a Republican motion to recommit with instructions failed 170-240 (with 15 Republicans and no Democrats voting for it), and final passage was 244-166, with 220 of 232 voting Democrats and 24 of 200 voting Republicans in favor [S7, S8, S9].
The Senate received the bill on November 5, 2007, and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, where no further action is recorded; the Congress ended January 3, 2009 [S5, S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies operating under the 1872 Mining Law kept royalty-free access to federal land and avoided new cleanup-bond and permit requirements. Taxpayers and western communities continue to bear abandoned-mine cleanup costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hardrock mining companies kept royalty-free access

sides.party_line_note: Passage was 244-166, with Democrats 220-3 in favor and Republicans 24-163 against; the failed motion to recommit split 0-225 among Democrats and 170-15 among Republicans [S8, S9].

industries.note: The bill would have ended the industry's royalty-free access to federal land, imposed an 8% gross-income royalty on new production, required permits and full reclamation bonds, and closed some areas to new claims. The industry's cost would have funded abandoned-mine cleanup and community assistance. Sources: S3, S4.

Taxpayers currently receive no royalty on hardrock minerals taken from federal land and frequently bear abandoned-mine cleanup and water-treatment costs; the bill would have redirected royalties and fees to reclamation and community accounts. Sources: S3, S4.

The Hardrock Community Impact Assistance Account would have funded public facilities and services in communities socially or economically affected by mining, and tribes could petition to withdraw culturally important land. Sources: S3, S4.
